opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting tensions in the field right now, and honestly I don't think there's a clean answer.

On one side, there's a very real temptation to chase specific benchmarks. You pick a task, coding, math competitions, some agentic workflow, and you can pour data and RL compute into it and watch the number go up. That's useful, and it's also how a lot of practical value gets delivered. But the question I keep asking is: did the model actually get smarter, or did it just get better at that particular shape of problem? Those are not the same thing, and sometimes you only find out months later when you look at how it behaves on something adjacent.

What's encouraging is that some tasks seem to transfer surprisingly well. Coding is the classic example. When you train a model to write and debug code carefully, you often see gains in structured reasoning more broadly: breaking problems into steps, checking intermediate results, being more honest about uncertainty. Math has a similar flavor. So certain tasks act almost like a curriculum for general capability, because the skills they demand are fairly universal.

Other tasks don't transfer much at all. They're more like learning a format or a set of conventions. You can get very good at them, and the model as a whole doesn't really move. Sometimes you even pay a tax elsewhere, a bit of narrowing, a bit of overconfidence, a style that leaks into places it shouldn't.

So the way I think about it is that task-specific improvement is valuable in two very different ways. One is direct: people need the model to do this thing well. The other is diagnostic and developmental: does pushing on this task reveal or strengthen something general? The best research bets are the ones where you suspect the answer to the second question is yes, where the task is a lever on something deeper like long-horizon planning, reliable self-correction, or grounding in real feedback.

And I'd add that the foundation still matters enormously. A stronger base model makes every downstream specialization cheaper and more robust. If the base is weak, task tuning feels like stacking things on sand. If the base is strong, a relatively small amount of targeted work unlocks a lot. So in the long run I see them as complementary, but I try to stay humble about which improvements are real generalization and which are just us getting good at grading ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says some task-specific training can strengthen general capabilities and describes those tasks as levers on deeper skills, benefiting foundation-model research overall.

r002.rationale: It says a stronger base makes targeted specialization cheaper and more robust, but does not state that steadily improving performance across new tasks and environments enables increasingly targeted methods.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that these two things are much more entangled than people assume, and the relationship has shifted over time.

Early on, there was a very clean mental model: pretraining gives you the general capability, and then you do task-specific work on top, and those are separate stages owned by separate teams. The base model is a kind of raw material, and the task work is shaping it. What we've learned is that this separation is mostly an illusion. When you push hard on a specific task, say math reasoning or coding or long-horizon agentic work, you usually discover that the bottleneck isn't the task, it's some underlying capability the model doesn't have yet. The model can't hold enough context, or it can't verify its own intermediate steps, or it doesn't know when it's uncertain. And fixing that thing lifts everything, not just the task you were targeting.

So I'd say specific tasks are how general capability becomes legible. You can't improve "intelligence" as an abstraction. You need a surface where the failure actually shows up, and tasks are that surface. The best task work is the kind where you're using the task as a probe, and you keep asking what the general version of this failure is.

But there's a trap on the other side too. If you only optimize for the task, you'll get the task, and you'll often pay for it elsewhere. You see models that become very good at benchmark-shaped problems and worse at everything adjacent, or that learn a shortcut that works on the evaluation distribution and collapses the moment the user phrases something differently. That's the signature of task improvement that didn't translate into capability. And I think the discipline is to always check: did the gain generalize to things we didn't train on? If it didn't, we didn't actually learn anything about the model, we just taught it a trick.

The other thing I'd add is that the direction of transfer isn't symmetric. General capability tends to make task work cheap. A model that's genuinely stronger needs much less data and much less scaffolding to pick up a new domain, sometimes just a good description. Whereas task work only occasionally feeds back into general capability, and when it does, it's usually because the task required something fundamental, like planning or self-correction. So if I had to allocate effort, I'd still bias toward the general side, but I'd use a small number of carefully chosen hard tasks as the thing that tells me whether I'm actually making progress or just moving numbers around.

r001.rationale: The response says that probing specific tasks can reveal underlying capability gaps, and fixing those gaps can lift performance beyond the target task.

r002.rationale: The response says stronger general capability makes learning new domains cheaper, but does not state that steadily reaching reasonable performance across new tasks and environments enables more targeted improvement methods.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re related, but they’re not the same thing. You can improve performance on a specific task by adapting the model very closely to that task—giving it better examples, a particular workflow, or more targeted training. That’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the foundation model has become more capable in general.

The key question is whether the improvement transfers. If you train a model to solve coding problems, does it also get better at breaking down unfamiliar problems, checking its assumptions, or correcting mistakes? If those abilities carry over to other settings, then the task has helped develop a broader capability.

So I see specific tasks as both training grounds and measurement tools. We need concrete tasks to make progress, but we also need to test beyond what we optimized for. Otherwise, it’s very easy to mistake getting better at a test for getting better at the underlying ability.

r001.rationale: The response describes specific tasks as training grounds that can develop broader capabilities when improvements transfer beyond the task.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that steadily reaching a reasonable performance level across new tasks and environments enables more targeted improvement methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re related, but improving a specific task doesn’t automatically mean the foundation model has become more capable overall. You can improve a task through very targeted training, better prompting, or engineering around the model. Those gains can be useful, but they may not transfer.

The more interesting question is: what did the model have to learn to get better? If it learned something reusable—how to reason through a problem, use evidence, or recognize when it’s uncertain—then a specific task can become a route to broader capability. If it learned shortcuts that only work within that task, the improvement is much narrower.

So I’d look at transfer: does the improvement show up on unfamiliar problems, including ones we didn’t optimize for? Specific tasks give us concrete feedback, but we need that broader testing to understand whether we’ve improved the foundation model itself.

r001.rationale: The response says that learning reusable skills through a specific task can lead to broader capability, and that specific tasks provide feedback about improving the foundation model.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that steadily reaching a reasonable level on new tasks and environments enables more targeted improvement methods.
